To summarize: This is probably the best game I've ever played. (* note: I have ~80 hours across another account). 

If you like Red Dead Redemption 2, Assassin's Creed for the history (but don't like it now as it's too grindy/repetitive), a less "arcadey" and more realistic Skyrim, immersive pretty landscapes, amazing soundtracks, and a great storyline with likeable characters - look no further. 

[u]Positives[/u]
- This game is a masterpiece in storytelling. Every mission feels handcrafted and interesting. There are no "fetch" quests, there's no grinding, my only complaint is that the story was too short (but to be fair it is like 40 hours). The main story was truly great, and not typical of most games - if you like real, human stories - this was great. Felt like all three Lord of the Rings movies in scale and depth.
- Every landscape feels cinematic. The level of detail in terms of culture and immersion is unmatched - the dev team has done an incredible amount of research to make the lore accurate to what it was back then. For example, Kuttenberg Castle was developed based on the modern-day ruins of the old one. The environments are loosely based on real areas in the Czech Republic. And you can experience everything in no stutter, thanks to no UE4/5. Definitely play on at least High settings on a good monitor - part of the charm for me was the visuals.
- I love that the game is realistic and combat is truly unique. The combat takes some time to get used to (this game has unique combat - it's not the usual point and click / button mash as in other games). But once you get used to it, you honestly don't want to go back - swordfighting feels truly skillful and satisfying. People do hate on the polearms, but I think the developers made them purposely bad - as they weren't exactly good weapons back then either.
- The characters are well written and memorable - you're invested in Henry's story, Hans captures youthful hubris. The Sigismund vs. Wenceslas rivalry and the ending is good.
- Going in, I knew that this series aims for realism in the sense that you start very weak then build your character up organically. That progression is one of the most satisfying things about this game. Furthermore, in doing so, you do everything realistically - e.g. forge swords by hammering them and cooling them instead of clicking a button that says "craft". This realism was unique, enjoyable and well executed. 

[u]Neutral / Negatives[/u]
- Yes stealth is bad - it's a roll of the dice and you can't reliably stealth kill. BUT that wasn't an issue for me - it's realistic, and this isn't meant to be played as a stealth game. 
- Some people have valid complaints that in certain instances the game leaves you in the dark to figure things out on your own, but for me that was part of the fun. Early game was frustrating as I hadn't realised how to save, but if you're able to just go along with that the game gets waay better once you learn to deal with the initial hurdles. My advice is let yourself figure some things out instead of relying on walkthroughs and for the game to hold your hand. Furthermore, if you don't like figuring out things you can always read some walkthroughs for those certain scenes. Don't worry about minmaxing is one thing I should have known going in - yes there is a 'bad' ending but it's only like a 2 minute clip. It's no big deal as you can watch it on YouTube. Just enjoy the game.
- On that note, the opening sequence I think is a filter. If you can get through it, you will enjoy this game. I died twice - it was a little frustrating, maybe this sequence could use a little more handholding.
- Combat can be glitchy sometimes, such as when fighting multiple enemies or fighting between elevations.

Overall, this was a fun, immersive game that had a wonderful story and scratched my itch of "they don't make them like they used to". Would definitely give it a 10/10 and highly recommend you play.

Over the weekend I started playing Kingdom come deliverance 2 on PC and I cam to realize this game basically pulled off what most of AAA games publishers already long forgot.

They created a fully realized world, super detailed with actually interesting quests and dialogue that on the same level as Witcher 3 side quests. Even small side quests could become like a 2 hours detour and they are actually interesting. Your choices in the game actually means something and could effect the world around you and how things developed and determine the end results of a quest. Cyberpunk 2077 tried that and based all of their PR on that notation but in reality they were not even close to what KDC2 pulled off here . Even how you look and what you wear and in what condition could effect how NPC will talk to you. This is something that has been long forgotten in modern video games where the only things that matter is graphics and cosmetics.

The combat is really refined now and works so much better than when the first game came out. The NPC reactions to hits and battles are also really impressive like when you pull off master strike or perry or an interesting combo they actually react to that.

on the technical side the PC ports works very well, no stuttering at all consistent frame rate and frame time while the world and the game looks very realistic. I am playing on i9 14900kf and RTX4080 16gb and able to get locked 60 fps in 4k on ultra. it's honestly so rare this days to get a good working PC port.
If you have a good gaming PC, you should very much check out this game, it's really a fantastic game.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II starts off quite slow, and I’ll admit the early hours require some patience. But if you push through, the game really opens up and becomes genuinely exciting. The developers have done a great job of making you feel like you’re truly living in medieval Bohemia — the atmosphere, world design, and daily life immersion are all incredibly well done.

Although I usually prefer games where I can create my own character, playing as Henry still works well. The narrative and plotline are engaging, and I’ve enjoyed following his journey. The combat mechanics are solid, with a satisfying amount of depth, and the gear and perk systems feel meaningful without being overwhelming.

I also appreciate having dialogue choices, though I found that many of my attempts tend to fail — maybe that’s just an early-game thing. Still, it adds to the role-playing element. One thing I really like is how the game creates moments where you suddenly become the centre of attention, often in embarrassing or reputation-damaging ways. It makes the world feel reactive, and it forces you to carry those consequences and work to prove yourself over time, which adds a surprisingly compelling layer to the experience.

Overall, it’s a very positive experience so far — immersive, challenging, and rewarding once it gets going, with a strong sense of place and character.

In my eyes, KCD 2 is one of the best games in many years — maybe even the best, for several reasons.

Reason #1 – It’s genuinely different

This is the biggest standout for me. The combat system, the meaningful consequences of your actions, the freedom in how you approach quests — everything feels fresh. In a world full of games that play the same, this one dares to be unique while still being incredibly engaging.

Reason #2 – Atmosphere and storytelling

The game captures medieval Czechia with impressive authenticity. There’s no need for zombies or other fantasy gimmicks — it’s pure, grounded, and immersive. The open world is massive, beautifully crafted, and truly alive. Unlike many modern open-world games where NPCs feel awkward or artificial, here they feel real. You can spend time doing everyday tasks or jump straight into grand adventures, and both feel natural. NPC stories, quest mysteries, and worldbuilding are simply brilliant.

Reason #3 – Czechia and its rich history

This one is personal. As a Czech player, I’m incredibly proud of Warhorse Studios for bringing our history, landscapes, and landmarks to life for the world to experience. Our country has so much to offer historically, and seeing it portrayed in such a modern, engaging form means a lot.

For me, this absolutely deserves GOTY.

My Thoughts on Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is extremely immersive is unlike any RPG I’ve ever played. The realism in the graphics engine, the craftsmanship of the world, the scripting, level layout, and 3D modelling are all on another level. The dynamic interactions, voice acting, and authentic regional accents really sell the setting and time period. Even the slang and terminology feel historically correct and enrich the experience.

Most quests feel like believable events you’d expect a knight, vagabond, bandit, or mercenary to be caught up in during that era. Yet they’re still woven seamlessly into the main narrative, keeping things engaging without feeling repetitive. I genuinely felt like I was building a real rebellion with actual people whose stories mattered. The tragedies that happen to some characters are genuinely impactful, and I found myself forming strong attachments to the friends and allies I made along the way.

You connect with Henry so much more in this sequel. His backstory hits harder, and this game does a great job showing his growth and maturity from the first game. For reference: I put almost double the hours into this compared to the first. I was shocked to see nearly 80 hours on my save before even reaching the second region. There’s just so much to do, and all of it feels immersive.

The new weapon-crafting and forging system is incredibly fun, realistic enough to match the time period but gamified just enough to avoid being tedious.

Combat is a bit easier this time, which is good in some ways; you can actually take on multiple enemies without the clunky feel of the first game. But sometimes it feels too easy, perfect ripostes can trivialize fights. Some added randomness or variety in fighting styles might help, so ripostes aren’t always so powerful. Still, the improved lock-on system is worlds better, making multi-enemy combat more fluid and less janky.

Cutscenes have improved massively. They feel far more cinematic, natural, and expressive than the original. The animations, staging, and amount of detail in each scene make the storytelling far more engaging.

As for DLC: in the first game they were hit-or-miss. This time around, it seems like Warhorse is taking more time and putting more care into each one. They’re still not Witcher 3–level expansions, but they’re looking stronger and more substantial. Hopefully future DLC continues scaling up.

The first game already did so much right, and this one expands on nearly every aspect. In my opinion, KCD2 deserves Game of the Year. I absolutely recommend it, and I’m excited to replay everything again in Hardcore Mode once all the DLC drops.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is everything I loved about the first game—just bigger, deeper, and even more immersive. From the moment you step back into Henry’s world, it feels like you’ve been dropped straight into a living, breathing medieval Bohemia. The attention to detail is unreal: the landscapes feel hand-crafted, the towns buzz with life, and even the smallest interactions carry weight.

What really sets this game apart is its commitment to authenticity. Combat is brutally satisfying, every swing has weight, and victory always feels earned. The story picks up without missing a beat, pulling you into political tension, personal growth, and moments that genuinely hit hard. And the role-playing depth? Incredible. Every choice feels meaningful, whether you’re deciding how to approach a quest or navigating the consequences of something you did hours earlier.

The game isn’t just immersive—it’s absorbing. One minute you're running a simple errand, and the next you're tangled in a chain of events that leads to a duel, a midnight investigation, or a chase through the woods. Somehow, it all feels natural and grounded.

If you’re looking for a medieval RPG that respects your intelligence, rewards patience, and delivers a story worth investing in, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 absolutely nails it. It’s one of the most engaging, authentic, and satisfying experiences I’ve played in years.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a phenomenal sequel that significantly improves upon the excellent foundation of the first game. If you loved the original, this is an even better experience.

It is highly recommended to play the first installment, Kingdom Come: Deliverance, beforehand to fully appreciate the story and characters.

The world is incredibly dynamic and alive, offering a sense of reality rarely seen in RPGs. The visuals are beautiful, making the new areas a pleasure to explore.

The game offers a huge degree of freedom, supported by a genuinely interesting main story and high-quality, non-repetitive quests.

The combat system is deeply rewarding and satisfying. It’s tactical, requiring you to think strategically, especially when fighting multiple skilled enemies. You truly feel like you are fighting for your life.

Dialogue is well-written, meaningful, and often very funny, adding great character to the world and its inhabitants.

This is a must-play for anyone who enjoys immersive, historical RPGs.

I love so so much about it, I love its commitment to realism and aversion to fantasy (I love fantasy, but the hard commitment to realism is a breath of fresh air). I love the character writing, I love how Hans grows on you like a mold, I love how naive and hopeful and just young Henry is, there’s so many gruff jaded protagonists that having him freak out at the mention of the devil or just blindly believe random sh*t or just refuse to compromise on his morals is so endearing to me. I love the world and systems for stealth and stealing and character schedules, just a pleasure to be in and play around with. But by far my favorite part of the game are the side quests, they’re so unique and fun, the rewards are universally bad but it genuinely doesn’t matter, you just go somewhere and you watch some weird, funny or creepy medieval drama unfold, and it’s different and interesting every time. I also love how your different character stats can also play into it New Vegas style.

I loved how small things in this game had a level of challenge to them.  You have to watch your characters hunger, and at the beginning of the game it's a bit hard to find food without stealing. Your equipment wears down (especially boots), and your character can stink if you don't visit the bathhouse.  I laughed when an enemy found me while I was crouching behind them just because they could smell how bad my character stunk. I also really enjoyed learning about medieval Europe as a lot of it is historically accurate with an in-depth codex’s detailing events, real noblemen, and general things like historical professions and the like. I could never in a million years have imagined that a game this hardcore and slow paced could have as few rough edges as KCD2.

The fact that myself, and seemingly most of the people that are still talking about it online drop 40-60 hours into the game before starting the first real main mission is testament to how well designed, integrated and engaging all of the systems in the game are, which for a game with such a large amount of very in depth systems is a straight up masterstroke of game design. I've played countless open world RPGs and no game has come close to getting me this deeply invested via its gameplay systems alone. Just existing as Henry, building up his stats and gear while also improving my own understanding of the game and combat evokes a feeling I can only compare to the "one more turn" feeling you get from the Civilization games. There is always something to do and a reason for me to want to do it and that feeling seemingly just never stops.

It's a lot like RDR2 for masochists and if Arthur was 15 again. It's not a "fun every minute" kind of game. It's immersive and challenging, and there's a great satisfaction loop as you improve at various things. I think it requires a bit more nuance and preparation than a lot of modern day RPGs, which can be frustrating to people expecting more of a Ghost of Tsushima type game, or a game with fights every 5 minutes. Let's say that where in RDR2 the immersion stuff felt rapidly like a chore here is linked to actual gameplay mechanics and not just for the sake of it. Personally, I think KCD2 does a great job of rewarding the extra effort that it asks of the player.

It's one of those games where the positives far outweigh the negatives. The game can be quite buggy especially in the second map, the story drags on in certain parts (especially those extended sections where you can't explore freely until you complete the quest), pacing is inconsistent, good loot is easy to obtain early game, etc. However, the writing, characters, voice acting, visuals, soundtrack, realism and detail this game has far compensate those issues. In a way it reminds me of The Witcher 3 10 years ago. I put about 100 hours into the game and don't regret a single minute of it. I'm looking forward to a second playthrough in the future, trying different choices and gameplay styles. It's GOTY contender for sure, though Clair Obscur has a strong case to win as well.

I have not felt like this about a video game since crawling out of the prison in Bethesda's Oblivion and discovering a sprawling world rife with adventure and nature. This game is not for everyone, the combat takes patience and finesse, it is a survival sim and you are not the chosen one and you will fail at conversations constantly, but this is a game for me and I'm so thrilled to have played it. I know I'm rambling here but the best comparison to make my point is Larian Studios: Divinity Original Sin 1&2 are some of the best games made for CRPG fans. Baldurs Gate 3 however is a game that creates CRPG fans. Similarly KCD1 was a very good game made for a specific niche of hardcore immersive RPGs. KCD2 I think has the potential to create fans of such games, in a way that I don't think we've seen since Skyrim.

In conclusion, I've never felt more immersed in the Middle Ages. The graphics are stunning, and the level of detail is astonishing. Everything just feels right. Even walking through the forest is so immersive it's breathtaking. This level of detail, combined with the vast possibilities the game offers, makes it an experience you don't want to miss out on! If you’re willing to sit down, take things slow, and just get lost in it, there really is no game that does it better in my opinion. I can wholeheartedly say that if you want to experience an amazing campaign set in a perfectly recreated version of life in 1403 Europe, give it a try you won't regret it.

KCD2 is easily my favorite game of all time. The game accounts for everything you do, down to each step and the weight you're carrying in your inventory. Your character learns skills in such a natural way -- start doing the thing, it's cumbersome, you don't feel very successful -- but you gain xp with each keystroke, even just for trying the thing without executing it perfectly.  All of the quests have a variety of ways you can  solve them, using  any number of the skills that you choose to build-- and your knowledge of the skill can come up  in any number of conversations , leading to interesting outcomes related to the things you've chosen to spend your time doing. It's been a very rewarding experience of "trying things for the sake of interest" (archery! blacksmithing! horse riding! religious scholarship! alchemy! etc) and, as you go about your characters' life, see the interesting ways that skills serve you in resolving conflict and discovering things about the world around you.

All the while, you're learning an incredible amount about medieval Bohemian life, customs, and historical events. Each time your character learns about something, it's stored in a codex that you can access at any time to learn more about the subject. I don't think I've ever learned so much about a real place and time in a digital, interactive environment as I have with KCD2.  The game had a whole swath of PhD history consultants credited.
The game marries complex systems with probably the most detailed immersive sim environment I've ever experienced.

It accounts for hunger, sleep, the clothes you're wearing (dirty? clean? damaged? smelly? style of clothing? Are you talking to a noble or commonfolk? etc), injury, bleeding, inventory weight, reputation, all conversation choices, etc. At first glance, it certainly sounds overwhelming, but the game puts loads of resources in your path to make the management of all these aspects a natural part of the gameplay loop, rather than stressful things to manage, or making you feel like "oh, god, a life sim?! I came to get away from real life!"

As for the environment, the game was rendered in CryEngine, giving it a different feel than Unreal and other popular engines.  Probably the best showcase for the engine is the environment/landscape art renders - truly beautiful, true to life (lots of fans on Reddit post 1:1 photo comparisons in Czech Republic, super impressive how close they are)

You can pick up and interact with so many things in the world.  Dropping items in the world  can lead other people to pick them up  and use them  if it catches their fancy.  NPCs follow full  schedules during the day.  You can kill  anyone, or do  a  pacifist run. The game respects all of your choices, and your actions almost always reflect in the narrative in meaningful ways. It's the most 'immersive' out of any 'immersive sim' ever.

In short, it really impressed me how much love and detail went into this game, and I can tell that these Czech devs were given lots of license to fill the game full with their heritage and history.

"I Spent 200+ Hours Getting Beaten Up in the Mud and Never Felt More Alive"

★★★★★ (10/10)

If you've ever wanted to experience what being a medieval knight is actually like—which apparently means getting knocked on your butt by farmers with pitchforks and spending more time maintaining armor than actually wearing it—then congratulations, you've found your new obsession.



The combat system had me absolutely fuming for the first 10 hours. I was getting my butt handed to me by bandits, my carefully planned attacks were failing spectacularly, and my stamina bar was basically a bully mocking me. Then—Chef's kiss—something magical happened. I stopped expecting button mashing to work, actually learned directional combat, and suddenly I felt like an actual swordsman instead of a drunk guy with a stick. Now pulling off a perfectly-timed master strike feels better than any video game achievement I've ever accomplished.


The Hidden Gems:
The horseback combat, the blacksmithing system that's weirdly addictive, the fact that you can fire crossbows while riding (which is hilariously overpowered), and the perks system that actually makes your character feel unique and specialized. Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 — A Timeless Medieval Experience

A Sequel That Elevates the Vision
Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 takes everything that made the first game special and refines it into a richer, more polished experience. It’s not about flashy fantasy elements or mythical creatures — it’s about immersing you in the raw, authentic life of medieval Europe. The sequel feels like stepping into history, where every decision, every duel, and every conversation carries weight.

A World That Breathes
The setting is one of the most convincing medieval worlds ever created in a game.
• 	Villages and towns bustle with activity — merchants haggle, peasants toil, guards patrol.
• 	Forests and countryside feel alive, with wildlife, hidden paths, and quiet moments of solitude.
• 	Castles and strongholds tower with grandeur, reminding you of the political and military struggles shaping the land.
What makes this world special is its authenticity. It doesn’t feel like a stage set for quests — it feels like a living society, where you are just one person trying to survive and make your mark.

Combat That Demands Skill
The combat system is challenging but deeply rewarding.
• 	Swordplay requires timing, stamina management, and precision.
• 	Archery is skill-based, with no magical aim assist — every shot feels earned.
• 	Mounted combat adds cinematic flair, letting you charge into battle with power and momentum.
Unlike many RPGs where combat is flashy and forgiving, here it’s tense, deliberate, and immersive. Victory feels like an accomplishment, not a given.

Storytelling Without Spoilers
The narrative is powerful, but what makes it shine is not the specific events — it’s the tone and themes.
• 	It’s a story about growth, resilience, and choices.
• 	Characters are complex, with believable motivations and personalities.
• 	Decisions matter, shaping relationships and the world around you.
You don’t need spoilers to appreciate how the game makes you feel: invested, conflicted, and immersed in a journey that feels personal.

Atmosphere and Presentation
The game’s presentation is breathtaking.
• 	Visuals: Realistic lighting, detailed environments, and cinematic cutscenes.
• 	Sound: From the clang of steel to the chatter of taverns, audio pulls you deeper into the world.
• 	Music: A sweeping orchestral score that adapts to your actions, heightening both quiet exploration and epic battles.
It’s not just about graphics — it’s about atmosphere. The game makes you pause, breathe, and soak in the medieval world around you.

Why It’s Great
• 	Authenticity: Few RPGs capture medieval life with such detail.
• 	Player Agency: Your choices matter, shaping the world in subtle and dramatic ways.
• 	Replayability: Multiple paths and outcomes encourage experimentation.
• 	Immersion: Every system — hunger, fatigue, reputation — adds depth without feeling like busywork.

Final Verdict
Without spoiling a single detail, I can say this: Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is not just a game — it’s an experience. It challenges you, rewards you, and immerses you in a world that feels alive and authentic. Whether you’re drawn to its combat, its storytelling, or its atmosphere, this sequel delivers one of the most memorable medieval role-playing journeys ever created.

Environments are beautiful, characters are well thought-out (as far as I got in the game), the story was interesting,  but the gameplay was the dealbreaker for me. Your choices don't matter. I dislike that no matter what you choose, you may end up with the same result anyway (the early encounter with the knights, the bar fight). The gameplay doesn't feel like it was made for PC at all. Hit boxes are also off when it comes to wolves, which doesn't help. The potion brewing is also quite hard to master. Conversations often go wrong and it can be hard to understand why.

There are some bugs too, like rabbits running backwards or upside down. Ruins my immersion.

The early quests where boring, especially finding Mutt. It's just a whole bunch of "go there, no go there instead, no go there instead etc etc" around the map. It gets old real fast, especially without a horse.

The game in itself is also not very helpful for a new player like me. I have no clue if I'm over my head until I get ambushed by 6 bandits and insta killed. It doesn't even seem like the enemies have a stamina bar, they can just wail on me as long as they like while I get exhausted after 5 swings/blocks. I also don't know what quests I am supposed to prioritize (or if I have enough skill for it). 

Yes, I might not be the most OP gamer but I would have appreciated an easier level or more balanced gameplay. Not just normal or hard.

Along with the first game, this is one of the most boring video games I've ever played in my entire life. And I've played A LOT of them.

It's as if they said "What are the most boring parts of linear games? What are the most boring parts of open world games? Let's combine them together!" and started to make the game with this vision. In the most boring setting they could think of. Nothing you haven't seen before in any other game ever made. No flavour. Nothing cool or extraordinary. Like the entire game itself.

The main character has the personality and charisma of a wooden stick. If you don't have a "character", which you don't, it's better to have a silent protagonist. None of the other characters are interesting or charismatic or have anything interesting or cool to say, either.

The dialogue is absolutely banal. Go outside right now, and talk to a total stranger about the weather or something. I can guarantee you, it will be more interesting than any cutscene or dialogue in this game. The writing is so amateurish that they don't even follow the "generic" conventions. Example: A stealth section or even a tutorial section can be used to expose the player to some information about the world. But nope, the guards just talk about their boring everyday lives as you sneak by them. The most amusing part of this game for me was seeing the store page, where it's tagged as "Story Rich". Now THAT, is rich. It's also tagged as "Atmospheric, Realistic, Immersive". None of these adjectives are applicable to this game whatsoever. Though maybe "Realistic" does apply, since the experience of playing this game is close to being as painful, boring and miserable as it must have been in Medieval Europe, in a mental and conceptual sense.

The combat system... Don't even get me started. Just play "Mount & Blade", "Chivalry" or "MORDHAU" to see how a proper medieval 1st person melee combat system is done. Kingdom Come feels like playing "Simon Says" compared to those games. And the rest of the game isn't interesting enough to warrant going "whatever, let's just play as an archer." and ignoring it.

All in all, I invite anyone who's a fan of this game to... play more video games. "Kingdom Come" does not fill any hole within any library of video games, unless there are enthusiasts of experiencing boring medieval life through the lens of a buffoon who's bereft of any personality and charm, while playing the most excruciatingly tedious parts of every RPG ever made.

I realized Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 isn’t a sequel. It’s a punishment simulator disguised as realism.

The developers seem to believe that “immersion” means watching your save files spontaneously disappear while you stand there, contemplating your life choices. Apparently, in this world, manual saving is a luxury and basic stability is a myth.

And don’t get me started on the combat. I could land a perfect headshot — physics, logic, and divine intervention all in agreement — yet the game smugly whispers, “No kill for you.” Then, like a divine joke, one random peasant with a stick blinks at me and I’m instantly dead.

This isn’t “hardcore realism.” This is frustration disguised as authenticity. Every encounter feels like the developers’ way of saying, “We studied medieval life and decided the best way to replicate it is through player suffering.”

At this point, I’d rather go outside, grab a real bow, and fight a windmill. At least the windmill won’t erase my save file.

If you enjoy watching your time evaporate, getting punished for precision, and being gaslit by game mechanics, this is the perfect experience. Otherwise, save yourself the headache — because the game sure won’t.

This like its predecessor puts a huge amount of emphasis in trying to be as much of a simulation as possible, I feel as if there have been some really popular games that have tried to do this, Red Dead 2 being the one that comes to mind the most for me, but even in those titles I feel as if this element of "realism" (if we can call them that) it's still streamlined in different ways to still retain the gameplay elements that actually contribute in making the game... well... fun, and engaging; rather than tedious and boring.

I'll give you an example.

In Red Dead 2 you can get clothing through stores and brew coffee, you can do this by exploring the stores or by going through a menu that's contextualized like you're looking through a catalogue; so this retains the "simulation" elements, whilst still mantaining the functionality of a game. If you want to brew coffee you can camp at any point during the wilderness, open a sub menu, and then play a very simple minigame where you see Arthur putting a coffee brewer on top of the fire, it's simple, straightforward, but still manages to provide you with the illusion of doing this activity.

Here? One of the first things you do is brew a potion, but for this you have to, not only collect the herbs, but then you have to grind them in a pestle and mortar, and then proceed to choose wine as the base of the potion, boil it to a certain point, control the different times of brewing using a sand clock... I mean... the whole thing is just so unnecesarily convoluted. 

Next activity?

Collect sacks and carry them around from a cart into a pantry... you have to do this five times at a snails pace, because they're trying to simulate the tediousness of this activity...

I mean... I just started it, but it seems as if the developers didn't really cared about wether the content they were putting here was engaging or fun, it serves more as a medieval simulation, rather than an actual game. Now if that sounds fun to you, then I guess you'll enjoy this, but for me... so far it's really not my thing, and I don't think that'll change in the future sadly.

EDIT: Welp, I kept playing it and... yeah, this design philosophy of "figure it out" doesn't do it for me the way it's handled here, after a while I needed a bed, so I find an inn, but they don't give me the option to sleep in a bed or rent a room? So I try to sleep in other people's bed, but they get angry if you do this... so I can't heal the health I loss when running away from bandits...

Again, understand this is all very "realistic" for some, but the whole game also seems antagonistic towards you at all times, even if you back out of selling and purchase menus without realizing any sort of deal, people get angry at you and you lose reputation? Come on...

THE COMBAT IN THE GAME IS BAD. Let's start off with that. The idea behind parrying your opponents moves and attacking opposite to their guard is cool. However, it often seems that where you swing doesn't even matter because the AI will block it seemingly at random, This makes parrying attacks the best style for sword fighting and even then the hits that connect seem random, and the parry icon doesn't always seem to appear when an enemy is attacking. Using the mouse to look around and be the way to decide where your hits go sucks bc I'll often find that it will just pull my focus off the person i want to hit and to a different enemy. The no indication for enemy health I can live with ig, but it makes combat feel really odd and unimpressive. like I've hit this dude 5 times in the head and it doesn't even seem like he's weaker or bleeding. 

POTION MAKING AND SIMILAR CRAFTING IS NOT THAT FUN. Finding herbs in the wild without really any way to tell them apart from the generic greenery other than remembering what it looks like is certainly an interesting game design choice. I personally thought it was fine and shops and dead bodies generally had the herbs i need for normal potions. But WOW actually making them is so unfun, the recipe book seems to always be just out of character sight so you can't just glance over to it to see what's on the pages, you have to move menus over to it whenever you forget a step. It's better to just write the instructions down in an actual notebook. It also just takes too much time, I don't want to be peeping for a quest for a solid 15 minutes trying to find the nearest patch of herbs just to run another 5 minutes to an alchemy station and spend another 10 minutes crafting all the potions because there isn't an instant menu for it once you've made a certain amount. 

THE BASE LAYOUT FOR CONTROLS IS WEIRD. The movement and weapon swapping buttons are perfectly fine, but the speech menus for NPCs is really bizarre. I mean why is shift+Q+# normal responses, but shift+alt+# is a different speech option, but effectively does the same thing as before.Why are they different controls, I don't understand it, the both say responses when a person talks to you. Also, if you just walk up to someone and press E it just doesn't talk to some NPCs as if they don't acknowledge your existence, but some will pop you into a conversation line. X for call horse and hold+x calls dog is fine, but why when i crouch does it do neither but instead distracts an enemy (sometimes).

UNFUN GAME-PLAY LOOP. I didn't enjoy the game-play loop overall. Needing potions to save unless I'm leaving the game is the dumbest thing in a video game ever. If it was sleeping or something or resting I can understand because it is a game that's pretty realistic, but why give me the option in the pause menu to save if it requires an in-game item to do it anyway. AND I HAVE TO BREW MORE POTIONS TO DO IT. The running is really slow, or it at least feels like it compared to riding a horse, and having to fully stop on the horse to have a different set of key-binds for controls is also just draconian. The slow movement while carrying LITERALLY ANY OBJECT is excruciating, like how bad would it be if i could run with that sack of wheat or dead body or at least move at normal speed. (ps LET ME USE MY HEALING POTIONS IN COMBAT, I DIDNT CRAFT THEM JUST TO DIE IN TWO HITS FROM A GUY WITH A SHIELD WHO STILL SEEMS TO RUN FASTER THAN ME... thank you)

RANDOM HUD QUIRKS. The inventory menu is weird too, like there are 8 tabs that all have information that it should be on maybe 3 or 4 tabs. Why are my player stats divided between 3 tabs when there is already a scroll bar on the tabs anyway. Why when I click or hover over an item does it not describe the item with a pop-out, but I instead need to click a side of the screen that shifts the camera over away from my inventory to tell me about the item then I need to click back into the inventory to see my full list. Why does my proficiency in a skill seem to not do anything when interacting with NPCs unless I choose the option they like. Why do I have 3 pieces of armor all in the same category but they all go on different slots. Why do i need a separate helmet to wear the helmet I want? Why do my bandages have durability that's separate from each-other but consumed on use?

Overall I would rate the game a 5/10. The story is really good, the NPCs have fun dialogue and a lot of it. The random quest adjacent NPC interactions are fun, like beating up a mail carrier who lot a letter so he doesn't get whipped is a cool side tangent. The introduction and cinematic scenes so far in the game are good as well. The scenery and environment is interesting and there are plenty of hidden locations to find. HOWEVER, ultimately a game is only as good as it's game-play and Kingdom Come: II just does not have it. The melee fighting is clunky and seemingly random, the crafting of basic items is atrocious, sneaking is not enjoyable and offers no real extra benefit vs just killing the enemy and stealing their stuff. The quests that seem like they should take place in one location have you running across the map to find someone only to run all the way back just to say you found them.

TL:DR If you are a story driven gamer this game will probably be fun for you, if you spend your time only with NPCs and foraging. If you are looking for a fun action packed exploration based RPG, go somewhere else you will be putting new holes in your monitor from getting frustrated at random groups of bandits that clap you back to 3 towns over because your attacks won't land.

The combat is lackluster, has poor responsiveness, and feels more jerky and slippery than smooth and forceful.
It feels like a M&B mod with Oblivion-esque UI that had the story fleshed out massively to where millions of people who didn't even know the Kingdom of Bohemia or the Cumans existed now do by virtue of this game's, and this game's predecessor's success; but ultimately failed to improve upon the combat in any real way from either the first game or M&B other than to add a fifth attack arc to the existing four.

Everything else about the game may be all well and good, and is to my limited experience; but the combat is so terrible even compared to Mount & Blade, which I would guess as the inspiration for the style of combat, that the game is a nuisance to play given that combat is offered as a viable option right from the tutorial by not only having it be listed as an archetype alongside Charisma and Stealth, but having the gall to put it as the initial option as well.
Hope you didn't tell the captain you were a soldier! Because if you did, you're rather fucked!
The speech-based option seems infinitely more viable given that combat is often avoidable anyway, and unlike other games where avoiding it is a choice you make; here the combat itself is so awful and clunky that it may as well be forcing you to avoid it. No wonder they added a dlc to give you high-end equipment early-on. You need it.
Even for a one-on-one you will struggle to block everything due to how finicky perfect-blocks are, despite the enemy rather often riposte-ing you.
Anything other than a one-on-one is basically impossible, as the game really wants to drive home how "only human" Henry is by making him extremely weak for how strong and effective he should be after the events of the previous game and the intervening time.

And you might stop and thing "well yes, that makes sense that it's hard to fight multiple people at once."
And you would be right.
If the game wasn't a sequel to another game where it's well established that your character is a capable fighter, even if you don't choose to have Henry be a career soldier; and yet this game expects it to be plausible that you can be dispatched and overwhelmed with ease by mediocre bandits with wood axes and peasants while you, a trained knight and bodyguard who has fought through hell just to survive, watch in dismay as yet another button input is delayed and your should-have-been perfect block leads to you being stun-locked to death yet again.

And then there's the stamina.
Now, I'm no trained knight or even in peak fitness; but I don't get lightheaded and woozy from swinging a sword five times. The stamina mechanic is just ridiculous, especially as Henry [i]is[/i] a trained knight and therefore likely [i]is[/i] in peak fitness, or near to it. It makes little-to-no sense that a few swings of a mere 1-3 pound short sword would tire Henry out unless he is intended to be asthmatic in the extreme and have hayfever year-round.

The developers have a clearly-ordained-and-intended way that you are supposed to engage in combat; that is by not doing so at all and fighting very defensively if you do.
And that is not fair to the players to try and force that upon them.
It's called [b]open[/b] world for a reason. That should include the whole game, mechanics and all; not just the world itself.

I stumbled across Kingdom Come: Deliverance in 2023. I knew nothing of Steam at the time. Because of KCD, I returned to gaming after a hiatus of many years. The urban landscape in the first game was as beautiful as a museum and I found myself visiting city after city just to examine the different churches. As a college professor who studied fencing as an adolescent, I loved the combat, as well as the immersive, historically-grounded story. While fighting in the first installment of KCD was admittedly difficult and required more practice than most games, I thought it was fun to acquire genuine expertise at both the basics (blocking, slashing, stabbing) as well as the more skill-based, advanced moves that players acquire through experience and training. KCD1 was not a perfect game. The story -- which initially concerns Henry's quest to avenge his parents and to recover a lost sword -- gradually loses focus and becomes an increasingly solipsistic "journey of self-discovery." The disappointing (and profoundly derivative) revelation of Henry's true origins was a narrative nadir from which KCD1 never quite recovered. And the game was, as many have pointed out, swarming with bugs, especially in crowded fight scenes. I never had the patience to complete one of the buggier, final quests ("An Oath is an Oath") so watched the game's irresolute "conclusion" on YouTube. 

Despite these shortcomings, I liked KCD1 enough that I looked forward to the sequel for months. I regret that I was disappointed by it immediately. I happily grant that archery is easier in the new version (though I am not sure that making things "easier" is a net gain for a developer that prioritizes realism to the degree that Warhorse does). Yet I found the alleged "improvements" to melee combat to be simplifications and dilutions designed to please the mob of weekend button-mashers rather than serious attempts to refine the system in KCD1. As Warhorse's approach to combat in KCD has become less realistic, its treatment of other matters (such as potion making) is now governed by an obsessive and tedious verisimilitude.  As others have pointed out, there are enough chores to do in the real world without inventing virtual chores in a fantasy version of medieval Europe. 

KCD2, alas, did not work for me. But most players seem to disagree with me on this one, and I wish them well.

------------[h3]120 Hours[/h3]------------

[h3]As a conservative:[/h3]
The game seems to not have much wokeness so far, though I haven't tried romancing anyone yet, apparently that's where it falls apart. I'm not talking about gay relationships, those obviously did happen. Apparently there are too many girl-boss type characters, which I haven't really noticed, though I can see how the lack of depth for basically every side character in the game could lead someone to this conclusion. It's quite clear Warhorse put more love into the first game than the second. 

Everything about KCD2 is more shallow; within the first few quests you are given a moral conundrum that is very upsetting and the outcome is nonsensical. An old lady who saved your life and risked her own by harbouring you from bandits asks you to murder a man who had "chased her out of the village". No evidence for this is presented to you and actually every NPC you interact with as part of this questline says he's done nothing but express dissent. It's obvious from what you are told and the quest's outcomes are that the "good" option is to commit murder because someone says things this hag doesn't like.

Another quest you can do around the same time has you re-uniting a quarrelling family of nomads. Again the "good" option is not morally sound, your options are to lie to a girl to get back her father's property, or to swindle her father.

I think problems like these are due to the developers only putting a surface level of attention to the quests and how the objectives weigh morally, whereas in the first game, you never felt like your only choice was to do a bad thing. Keep in mind the problem isn't that you have only bad options to get what you want; the problem is you literally cannot be a good person in this game and also complete the quests that are presented to you. Indeed, it feels like you are playing as a complete sociopath who can think of no option but to swindle and rob people, which is this game's biggest problem. I think this is due to a lack of depth and not necessarily some woke agenda, which I wont deny is rampant among basically all modern media.

[h3]As a gamer:[/h3]
KCD2 is very nice to look at, even though it is clearly still using the same skeleton as KCD1, almost all visual and surface level problems with the game are fixed. It also adds smithing, which is fun for a few minutes, until progressing with that leads you into yet another morality trap. That problem seems relegated to side-quests though, not sure if you can beat the game without completing them or not.

The good things about KCD2 stop at the surface. They fixed master strikes and clinches (sort of), but that comes along with the combat being a shadow or a knock-off of the first game. You have less options, the animations are more stale and there seem to be fewer. Even with all negative perks, you level up to strength 20 in no time at all then combat is the same as KCD1, where you can just run enemies over, except the enemies will now wait their turn to attack you.

Basically every game mechanic has been made more simple. You can always repair your gear from a very low craftsmanship level. They removed the pressure mechanic from sharpening, so now in order to make meaningful progress sharpening, you practically grind it on the edge like a dimwit. Lockpicking is more level based than skill based. Stealth is now Skyrim stealth, nobody is carefully watching you in the middle of the night from their bed, nobody is ever going to connect the dots unless they catch you in the act, oh and now we can do the biggest copout of all stealth mechanics; throw a fucking rock; must've been a rat. In exchange, you can now craft your own weapons... While wearing full plate and wielding a broadsword and heater shield, so why would you need new weapons? Sure it earns you money, but so will the three times you encounter bandits in high-end armor robbing merchants and villagers on your way from Zhelejov to Troskowitz. Which is yet another thing they dumbed down.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2: A Hyped-Up Pile of Medieval Manure That Left Me Seething
2/10 – Four Hours of Bullshit, and It's Already 2025's Trash Crown King. I promise you if there are any white knights of this game who this this game is remotely good, you're  either fucking delusional or a fucking troll. 

Look, I never played the original Kingdom Come: Deliverance, but I'd heard nothing but glowing things about it—gritty realism, deep RPG immersion, a fresh take on history without the fantasy fluff. Warhorse Studios had the hype machine cranked to 11 for the sequel, promising a polished epic that'd top charts. So I dove in, wallet open, expectations sky-high. After four rage-fueled hours, I uninstalled with a bitter taste and a fresh grudge against every influencer who shilled this trash. What a goddamn disappointment—this isn't evolution; it's a devolution into frustration porn, with every system screaming "screw you" at newcomers. I can't believe people hyped this up like it's the second coming. I must be getting old because kids nowadays eat up slop like this and call it genius. It's the worst game of 2025, a sluggish, buggy slog that gatekeeps harder than a velvet rope at a peasant ball. Steam forums are littered with early dropouts like me, calling it "literal hardcore boredom." Warhorse, you owe me a refund and an apology.

Melee Combat: Clunky Swings That Make You Want to Quit Mid-Fight
Combat? What a joke. They touted "refined" directional attacks, but it's a glitchy mess where Henry's flailing feels like fighting through pudding—swings whiff on unarmored goons with zero impact, hitboxes ghost you, and stamina drains like you're sprinting uphill in plate mail. Died eight times to a basic bandit in the prologue, each one a fresh hell of unresponsive inputs and stuttery animations. It's not skill-based; it's RNG roulette punishing your patience. [X user @calmandnorm: "steam won't let me post my review so here are my thoughts on Kingdom come deliverance 2 VERY BAD"] Four hours, and I still suck at it—feels like the game's laughing at me.

Save System: Saviour Schnapps? More Like Saviour Scam—Hours Wasted in Vain
Saving's the devil's work. No autosaves, just hoard those piss-poor Saviour Schnapps like your life's on the line (spoiler: your progress is). Ran dry after two saves, dumped an hour into a side hustle—haggling, dodging, the works—only to eat an ambush and reload to square one. It's paranoia fuel, not immersion, forcing you to babysit inventory over enjoying the world. Metacritic's negative brigade calls it a progress-killer, and after my wipeout, I get it—pure sadism in 2025.
Stealth System: Crouch All You Want, But Guards Are Cheating Bastards
Stealth's a farce. Shadows? Useless. Light armor preset? Still clomps like an elephant on cobblestones. Spent 30 minutes creeping a camp—crouch-walking, breath held—only for a guard to "hear" me through a bush from 50 yards out. No feedback, just instant alerts and chases. It's over-punishing without the tools to succeed early on, turning tension into tantrums. [Reddit gripes: "the game loses a lot of what makes it so immersive once your Henry becomes strong... but getting there? Agony."] Zero wins in my playtime—hype lied.

Pickpocket System: RNG Hell That Begs for Constant Reloading
Pickpocketing? Laughable. Sneak up, charge the wheel, pray the timer doesn't screw you mid-rummage. Items shuffle like a rigged casino—grab air half the time, get caught on a full success. Even basic marks wake up glitchy, no skill mitigating the dice roll. Perks tease fixes, but who grinds for that in hour two? [X rant echo: Players "sucked at and misunderstood" the mechanics, per one fed-up poster] Three fails, zero gains—trash.

Map & UI: A Bloated, Foggy Nightmare of Feudal Frustration
The map's a joke—vague scribbles with quest pins lost in fog, forcing endless menu scrubs to orient. UI? A bloated beast: tabs on tabs for gear, herbs, presets that lag mid-swap, crafting a mini-game from hell. Sluggish loads and frame chugs make exploration feel like wading through tar. Bugs compound it—NPC clips, frozen quests—turning beauty into blight. [NeoGAF: "Slow and lethargic, sometimes to a fault."] No wonder it's "disappointing" across the board.
Story hints at betrayal and grit, but the prologue grind buried it under tedium. World looks lush till a horse-physics fail yeets you off a cliff. Patches? Maybe, but the core's rotten for fresh blood like me. Hype was a scam—kids lap this up, but us olds see the emperor's got no clothes.

TL;DR: Hyped trash with whiffing combat, scam saves, broken stealth/pickpocketing, and a UI/map from 2005. 2/10. Worst of 2025—devs, fix your shit. **Edit:** Yeah, no. Hit registration is inconsistent, and you are forced back to being just as bad at combat as Henry was in KCD1 just to make the game "challenging". Continuing on this vein, the best way to win fights are with master strikes, but Henry for some reason acts like he hasn't spent an entire game before wearing any armor or sword fighting and lasts about 4-5 swings before he's gassed out and needs to breathe (even without wearing armor). Generally your best bet when fighting is just to parry everything, maybe get a master strike if the game feels generous, then wail on the NPC when they're gassed out. In short, the 1v1 fights feel boring. If you're fighting more than one person then it just depends on how lucky you are since the NPCs like to teleport through themselves to hit you through other NPCs

There are multiple instances where you have little to no control and are put into extremely frustrating situations for no real good reason. For example, as you're on the verge of entering Act 2 you are forced to fight a battle with no armor, and if you try to equip armor picked up from fallen foes the game just goes "lol no go yank your pizzle".

Narrative is a downgrade from the first game and has even more significant plot holes and is plainly predictable. The story is not that rewarding for time investment or how much frustration it puts you through. KCD1 had issues with random bandit encounters and they have made it even worse. You literally can have just started the game and have absolutely nothing, and you will randomly encounter 2-6 bandits and one of them will be wearing platemail. The game likes to tell you you can run, but it rarely works. The AI also does not have proper scaling - bandits are just as good of swordsmen as lords.

Lastly there are some stability issues with the game even running on a "launch a spaceshuttle" grade computer. Audio randomly doesn't work in cutscenes, you'll also get screwed up lighting, or some instances where the entire screen randomly goes black in one specific spot.

All this aside, the game is beautiful. It has that going for it at least.

This game feels like it was made by two different studios. One wanted to make an uncompromising medieval immersive sim for sickos, the other wanted to make a pseudo-AAA 2000s-style linear cinematic game for as broad an audience as possible. KCD1 had a lot of the first thing and a bit of the second thing, in a way that added up to a flawed but special gem of a game that I loved a lot. After wrapping up the story I'd often boot it up just to hang out, ride around, go to a beautiful church.

In KCD2, the mouthbreathers won out. Much of KCD1's systems are recreated here, but everything is put towards a massive and interminable main quest so boring and stupid I had to force myself to keep playing in the hopes that Kuttenberg would be worth it. The dialogue and characters are painful. I'm asked to embody and care about the bizarre and myopic revenge quest of an extremely boring and horny asshole with a puzzlingly contemporary haircut. Apparently I'm best buds with Hans Capon, and my ability to hang out in this lovingly crafted rendition of medieval Bohemia is being held ransom by literally dozens of hours of straight-to-DVD buddy cop bullshit with this character I tolerated in KCD1 but grew to utterly loathe here. 

KCD1 wanted to be more like this, but lacked the resources for 8-hour railroaded main quests and lavish cutscenes. This was to its enormous benefit. Left to my own devices, I was able to role play myself in a medieval world. Things like the combat system that forced you to learn it or the fact that you had to literally learn to read thinned out the membrane between player and player character. It was the kind of game I'd wanted to play since I was a kid imagining what videogames might be like. 

In KCD2, there is never any chance to forget that you are playing Henry, and I don't care about Henry. Henry is a stupid person's idea of an interesting and realistic main character for a medieval RPG. I don't give a shit about him or his stupid dead stepdad. The game has no interest in getting me to care, and just assumes that I will feel the way it tells me I feel. His quest feels so much like a budget 2000s action movie that they even try to make a catchphrase happen—it's all in Latin, except for the word "fucking." 

And you can't go inside the fucking churches!

Review of Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 left me with very mixed feelings. On one hand, the game tries to be realistic; on the other, many design choices end up being more frustrating than enjoyable.

Graphics and World

The graphics aren’t photorealistic, but they’re realistic enough to feel bleak. Most landscapes look like average flat European countryside — mundane, dull, and unremarkable. I have a similar forest outside my window, and there’s nothing there except trees and grass, which is exactly how the game feels. There’s very little visual variety, and finding a genuinely beautiful place for a desktop screenshot is surprisingly hard. I expected something more picturesque — surely there must be more scenic locations in Bohemia.

Cutscenes and Animations

The longer you play, the more irritating the cutscenes and animations become. Watching your character pick a flower or prepare a potion for the hundredth time is exhausting. Alchemy is downright painful: the camera shakes, causing near dizziness, and the animations drag on forever. Sharpening or forging weapons is equally tedious — it’s almost impossible to tell visually whether a blade is sharpened or not.

Cutscenes often don’t match what’s happening in the game. In the middle of a fight, the game suddenly triggers a cinematic where the protagonist is wearing completely different clothes and holding a crossbow I never used. Worse, even if you defeat all enemies, the script may kill NPCs anyway — just because that’s what the story demands.

AI and Stealth

The AI behaves erratically. Sometimes enemies fail to notice you at point-blank range; other times someone shoots at you through walls or from another village entirely. At one point I discovered that guards in a castle didn’t notice me crawling right in front of them.

Stealth is broken: sometimes you’re “required” to be seen by the plot, no matter how stealthy you were. I stole a sword from the swordsmiths’ guild without anyone seeing me, but the cutscene accused me anyway.

Progression and Perks

Progression relies almost entirely on skill levels — perks hardly change gameplay at all. If your level is high enough, everything becomes trivial: locks open easily, guards fail to see you, enemies can’t perform master strikes, and everyone agrees with you in dialogue. At least levels go up fast — I was playing as an archer, but after a few encounters with bandits I raised my sword skill enough for the sword guild quest.

Bandits also become absurd: early-game ragged thugs later get replaced by fully armored knights. Historically, full plate armor was insanely expensive — this is far from realistic. In fact, you don’t even need to buy armor: just fast-travel across the map, and the game will likely throw you a pair of “random” enemies conveniently wearing level-appropriate expensive gear.

Combat System

The combat system — and, really, the entire gameplay loop — hasn’t changed much since the first game. It feels like the same game with a “Part 2” sticker on it. First-person view is a questionable choice for sword combat. Human vision has around 120° FOV plus peripheral perception, which no game (even in VR) can replicate. Here, your view is restricted, your character’s hands block half the screen, and enemies hit you from all sides.

Animations are too long, and enemy master strikes are random, untelegraphed, and unavoidable. That’s extremely frustrating. Meanwhile, if you just stick to “block–attack,” you can win even a sword tournament — which makes the combat boring. I did exactly that despite my low sword level.

Dialogues

There is an overwhelming amount of dialogue. Sometimes it feels like the developers forgot about pacing entirely. The success of games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring shows that fewer words and better gameplay often work much better.

Conclusion

The game starts off strong with its difficulty and atmosphere, but the deeper you get, the more disappointing its casualness and mechanical limitations become. It’s long — very long — but the longer you play, the more monotonous it feels. I have absolutely no desire to replay it, and honestly, even finishing it once was a challenge.

I expected much more from Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2.
In the end, it’s a beautiful concept executed in a very uneven and at times downright frustrating way.

After 30 hours of playing, i find it hard to say i love this game. Perhaps the demographic this game aims at is those who can find fun and pleasure in an ultra realistic video game in which you are constantly dragged back by all sorts of UNNECESSARY little things. For example, I understand that I cannot sprint when I am overloaded, but why can't I ride a horse? Is it too heavy for the poor horse? In that case, why can I put tons of things on the horseback if they are too heavy for me and i don't wanna discard them? Where is the weight limit now?

Beside that, I simply cannot find any excitement in the map exploring part. The exploration mechanic feels like a combination of The Elder Scrolls and The Witcher 3, by which I mean if somebody mentioned a spot, it is marked on the map, then you can go for it and in every human gathering (villages, tents, towns) there's a chance to find some quests.

Speaking of the quest, the quest design in this game is BORING. No matter it is a main quest or a side quest, they all follow the same structure: Talk to someone, get a quest, and this quest requires you to talk to another one in a village far away (this is absolutely torturing when you are overloaded). When you get that village, that guy says OK I can help you, but I need you to do something for me first. Wanna know more information? Talk to another guy! Then you run to another spot... This stupid cycle runs through all the mission in the first map. I'm not sure if I can make it to the second one. I feel like a errand boy or a clown being played. Apart from that, goals of these quests are BORING as hell. Most of them are about FINDING: find a string, find a document, find lost sheep, find my missing daughter, find a bandit camp, find a lair to kill some wolves... If it is what a real medieval life is, I'd rather quit and play something less realistic. For anyone who thinks I'm overstating this, just check how many 'find's are there in your mission list.

Last but not least, developers are very cunning to prevent gamers from refunding. In the first two hours of playing, the only period when you can actually play this game is about 15 minutes. The remains are all cutscenes. THERE ARE TOO MANY CUTSCENES. That is too say, when I could finally PLAY this game and realised it was not for me. It was too late.

To be fair, there is improvement compared to its predecessor. Graphics are astonishing. Optimization is outstanding. Battle mechanic is unique and engaging. Some of the plot is humorous. Still, I regret spending my money on this game and I hope you won't make the same mistake.

I will finish this game because I love Henry, but I really cannot recommend it if you enjoyed the first one. Granted, it feels the same, plays the same and it's at the same level of immersion and realism. So if that's what you're interested in, go for it.

But, the storyline is nowhere near as flowy and interesting as the first one. It doesn't hit the same. Henry is in a weird place among the nobles. Everything feels annoying. Having to bear Capon for so many hours at the beginning of the game was a complete chore. Opening the map feels terrible because it takes a while to load. The cities, especially Kuttenberg, are almost intraversable, there are walls everywhere. The map is unhelpful most of the time, you have to walk miles to find a door that allows you to get to your destination. And, the main quest feels like an MMORPG, where you unlock a big stage of the storyline and are thrown into some countless hours of "side" main quests.

It lost the magic of being some dude from a small village, thrown in things much bigger than him and that allowed you to touch the ridiculousness of the people that inhabit medieval times. Now you're much more of an errand boy for the nobility.

Plus, if you want to be a scumbag then this game has it in for you. First of all, guard interaction after crimes is bugged AF. It has happened to me many many times that I fight a guard, only for it to surrender and then spiraling me into not being able to deal with the guard, not being able to kill the guard, or bringing me to an endless loading screen if I try to speak to it. Then, if I wanted to rob the entirety of Kuttenberg at night, with NOBODY SEEING ME, walking to the inn to sleep and the morning after I am automatically labelled as a thief????

All in all, I hope you won't, but for me this game has been a chore and I'm only driven by inertia and because I want to see where Henry ends up. But I'm not enjoying it that much. If you think you can do the same, maybe buy it in some years, or during a big sale.

I don't really understand the hype and positive reviews around this game.  If I could request a refund at this point, I would.

I spent the first 2 hours going through the intro sequences, with lots of scripted story to set the scene etc. and the dialogue was rather wooden and un-emotional, although the characters can be funny at points they seem to rely on lots of meaningless swearing.

After this, (and conveniently after Steam's refund timer), the real game begins, and there are many frustrations.

The save system leaves me questioning the design choices immediately, I'm not allowed to save unless I brew some potion that lets me, BUT I can "save and quit" at any point, leading to moments where I just need to quit to save and then load the game again.  Extremely pointless.

The combat is rather static, wooden, doesn't feel realistic or dynamic in any way.  It feels like something from the old era of gaming like Gothic etc.  It's just a matter of block/parry/attack rinse and repeat.

Then there's a forced first-person-view.  Why?  I want to see my character and the armour I've equipped, and I don't like all the forced camera movements in FPV when doing EVERY SINGLE ACTION.  it's like press a button, wait for 2 seconds while the camera moves around weirdly before you can do anything else.

As well as this, there are a lot of weird key binding choices, like sometimes I have to just press ESC to cancel something and other times I have to hold ESC for 1 second?  The same with E, or whatever.  Why?  This is confusing and un-intuitive and completely non-standard for PC key bindings.

And to top it all off, once I had managed to actually get to grips with some of the game systems and kill a small camp with 3 bandits in it near the starting area, I loaded myself up with their weapons and armour then proceeded down the hill to find 3 "wild dogs".  I got my ass absolutely beaten raw by these three wild dogs.  A man in armour, with swords, can't beat 3 dogs.  Right.

I also have issues with the stealth system, lockpicking, item equipping (you have 3 sets of equipment, and all of it ALSO stays in your inventory for maximum clutter), item stat comparison, and the combat system.  All of them feel clunky and at times like I'm not in control: the character and/or the UI feel unresponsive during actions quite a lot.

As a point of comparison with all of the above, I've been playing a lot of Mount & Blade 2 recently, and let me tell you that game does a lot of these things right, and overall has a MUCH better feel to playing it than KCD2.  It has a great first, and third-person views.  Amazing fluid and fast feel to the combat, 3 armour sets you can actually equip properly without cluttering up your inventory, and an easy to understand stat comparison for equipment.

So, I've modded this game now so I can save any time I want, and I have an optional TPV (which is pretty bad because the game hasn't been designed for it) but I'm hoping I can struggle my way through to find this supposedly "game of the year" content that people are going on about.

So far, it's very pretty, but every other thing about the game has frustrated me and feels clunky.  I will see how far I can get, but really not finding myself compelled to come back to play.  I unfortunately wouldn't find myself recommending this to my friends.

I bought this game because I had played and enjoyed the first one. At the time I had acquired and tinkered with KCD1 it was an enjoyable experience, almost (if not entirely) bug-free. Heard it was a buggy mess on release. I guess I got lucky.

On the other hand, KCD2 was a buggy mess to the point it rendered the game a very miserable experience.

I enjoyed the storyline and its side quests. As far as I am concerned, from Brabant to Zizka, from Kuybenka to the Dry Devil, the characters are memorable. Kudos to the writing team. Living in that historical period, finishing the story from the first game...getting to see interpretations of characters like Jan Zizka that I've read in the history books...if this was a movie, i'd happily rewatch it over and over. 

Gameplay-wise howver, as I mentioned earlier, the game was a buggy mess. From getting trrapped in pools of water to either getting stuck in doorways or watching npcs get stuck in the same frame (often getting me killed as a result).  I've seen horses (not my own) randomly spawn atop castle walls, for reasons?! And who couldn't forget the AI's ability to perceive the players actions through windowless walls, when he is making no noise in the room. Or that uncanny ability to spot a cadaver from the other side of the map and run towards it. 

Not to mention the combat issues. Reloading a handgun (or pistole as it is technically called in that era) is more often than not a nightmare. Standing on flat ground to reload? I get stuck in the endless loop of my character putting the gun barrel up to reload, then raising the gun up and putting it down again. Stopping the reload and re-attempting it doesn't work. Sometimes the solutions is to move to a different flat patch of grass or tile. 

The bigger issue for me, as a keyboard and mouse user, is the melee combat. If I had a penny for every time my weapons would slice through the opposition and not do damage, i'd be a millionaire. This is not a armor issue, but a hit-box problem that I've seen time and time again. Furthermore...clicking the buttons to attack, dodge or defend don't always work. So I end up dying more times than i should because the command lines are not working as they should. 

I have to complement the AI's heat-seeking missile skills. When I perform the perfect dodge to the left or the right, the AI is still able to ignore the dodge and deal a lethal blow. If I dodge backwards and technically am outside the range of a shortsword, for instance, the AI nonetheless is able to hit me. 

The last issue I have is with the armor. Swords are supposed to be great against anything that doesn't have heavy armor (the higher the armor rating, the less effective the sword)...that is the case when i strike an npc in full battledress, from helmet to plate armor. Yet the AI, with a sword, can cleave through 70+% of my health bar in a single strike (talking regular attack, not a master strike) through plate armor. 

Gameplay currently was demoralizing to the point of causing stress. The story was great (though admittedly I found the ending for Istvan Toth to be a bit underwhelming, haha).

Going to let the game cook for a while more. Then try again. This was a first playthrough. Took some lessons from it. Maybe things will be better in the second playthrough. As of right now, having completed the main storyline, I want to shelve the game and forget about the issues before re-experiencing it.

I bought the Gold Edition of this game after being blown away by its spectacular trailer and stunning artwork. Unfortunately, I fell for the classic case of judging a book by its cover — and ended up paying full price for it. Once launched, it became clear that the trailer was heavily pre-rendered and not representative of the actual gameplay. The graphics feel outdated, comparable to games from 2011, despite the game being quite demanding on system resources.

The combat mechanics show some promise but are ultimately underdeveloped, clunky, and uninspired. Most battles take place during sieges, and the combat system lacks proper support for fighting multiple enemies at once, which quickly becomes frustrating. The game is divided into two acts: the first is engaging and encourages you to keep playing. The second act, though larger in scale, feels empty and dull. Continuing beyond Act One felt more like a chore, and it's clear the developers cut corners toward the end. What a shame.

I wouldn’t recommend buying this game at full price. It feels highly unfinished and lacking in proper development. If you're curious, wait for a sale—and definitely skip the Gold Edition. Even after finishing the main story, I couldn’t bring myself to complete the DLC. It’s just plain boring.

EDIT (Final thoughts after completing the game):

After finishing Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2: doing every task, side quest, and side activity - I have some mixed but definitive conclusions. The game starts off incredibly strong. The writing is tight, the world feels wide open, and the level of detail is frankly astonishing. It gives you the illusion of limitless freedom, and for a while, it really feels like you're inside a living, breathing medieval world.

But somewhere around the Kuttenberg main quests, the seams start to show. Voice acting quality dips noticeably—some characters sound like they were recorded on a webcam mic by budget Fiverr freelancers. The quests begin to drag, and worst of all, they include hidden, progress-breaking decisions that aren’t communicated clearly. By that point, I stopped feeling immersed and started playing out of “FOMO,” afraid to turn in quests or even talk to NPCs without saving first or Alt-Tabbing to a quest guide or reddit post. (Thank god for the save-anywhere mod.)

The ending was... a disaster. Cringe-inducing. A good writer knows when to stop, and this one didn’t. The whole "bad/good ending" premise is misleading. There’s no impactful branching conclusion like The Witcher or even Metal Gear Solid: Twin Snakes. Just a strange dream dialogue and a flat, forgettable finale that left me thinking: That’s it? That’s what I spent dozens of hours building up to?

All in all, I can’t recommend this game to most people. especially not if you’re looking for a coherent, satisfying narrative. That said, there are moments where this game truly shines: scenes with von Aulitz, Adder, and several side quests are genuinely unforgettable. But those moments don’t reflect the bulk of my 215 hours.

The save system is another major flaw. I get what the developers were going for, but restricting saves, or forcing players to save constantly - ultimately pulls you out of the role-playing experience and reminds you you're just "playing a game."
