I feel extremely disconnected from this game...

The physics engine is a complete mess. A 20-year-old guy jumping down from a height of 2-3 meters with preparation still loses 1/4 of his health—does he have osteoporosis? Various obstacles as low as half a meter, or even 30 cm, cannot be climbed over, even while wearing light armor. Jumping against a wall often results in being bounced off in the opposite direction. Even games from 10 years ago had better physics engines than this.

Now let's talk about the leveling system. If you don’t install weapon mods or mods to reduce experience gain, by the time you finish the first map, you can easily reach level 20+, even without learning skills from NPCs. The game’s balancing is completely broken, making combat utterly uninteresting.

Speaking of combat, throughout the entire playthrough, not a single fight left a lasting impression on me. Many battles are even easier than fighting a fully armored roadside bandit at the very beginning without any equipment.

Okay, okay, I know some "die-hard fans" will say that this game is not about combat, but rather about immersion and role-playing. So, let's talk about that. The game’s economy is completely broken. The profits from stealing—or crime in general—are so high that if you don’t engage in criminal activities, you won’t even make 10% of what you would by committing crimes. However, choosing not to commit crimes provides no positive feedback. The game's crime tracking is also bugged—killing bandits or looting corpses is often falsely recorded as theft under Henry’s stats. Many times, I was just forging weapons in town, and suddenly, my theft count increased. Since I aimed for a crime-free playthrough in later runs, I became extremely sensitive to these statistics. But isn’t playing as a lawful, chivalrous Henry supposed to be a valid option? If you choose not to commit crimes, every time you leave town, you must be extremely cautious and save in advance—not because you fear bandits, but because you're worried about wrongful crime stats. Sometimes, after progressing several hours into the story, I check the stats and find mysterious theft records, forcing me to go through multiple save files to pinpoint when it happened. This makes it impossible to react naturally to random encounters, because just approaching them might get you flagged for a crime.

The absurd crime system. Helping a shepherd kill wolves and butchering them is considered looting corpses and gets you wanted for a crime. And don’t even get me started on looting after killing bandits—just touching their corpses counts as a crime! Warhorse, did you guys actually study medieval history? Looting the enemy was common practice in medieval battles, from the 1204 sack of Constantinople by the Crusaders to the Swiss mercenaries and Teutonic Knights. Which church or organization considered looting the dead on the battlefield a crime? Many abandoned camps and bandit hideouts have chests, and as long as you don't use a key to open them, it’s considered a crime—what kind of logic is this?

Okay, okay, "die-hard fans" might argue that Henry, as a devout 15th-century man, believes looting corpses is immoral. Fine, but does immorality equal crime? I personally think prostitution is immoral, but does that mean prostitution equals rape?

There is one more thing that deeply disturbs and disgusts me, and I sincerely hope this is not Warhorse deliberately pushing political correctness. If it is, then this kind of political correctness is even more horrifying and repulsive than LGBTQ+ representation or body diversity. The issue is that John Zizka’s mercenary forces, as well as the church assassins in the HERMIT quest, are categorized as civilians.

Look at what’s happening in the Middle East right now—how many bandits and terrorists claim to be civilians while preaching their so-called "noble ideals," all while committing indiscriminate violence against actual innocent people? Isn't this exactly the same as Zizka’s mercenary forces? Even Zizka himself admitted that his troops were a mixed bag, including criminals and even outright bandits. In the game, these NPCs are clearly labeled as bandits, yet when you follow the proper quest flow and kill them, they are counted as civilian casualties in the statistics.

I really hope this is just a bug in the statistics and not some kind of political statement, because that would be absolutely terrifying. Zizka’s forces actively set up ambushes and launch attacks, yet killing them somehow counts as murdering civilians?

The game falls off a cliff in terms of enjoyment in the second half. NPC interactions can be frustrating because it's ride or die with your decisions. No chance to communicate at all. A single misunderstanding can lead to death of great characters, and it's on your hands. The devs seem to want you to feel bad about yourself constantly.

Pros

- Great deal of flexibility with how you want to play the game. Lots of skills, weapons, etc.
- The voice acting is decent.
- The graphics are decent.
- Lots of different side material to try out (hunting, alchemy, dice game, etc).

Cons

- The pacing of the game is all over the place. The tutorial alone is like 4 hours long. Even main quests get stretched out for so long.
- Your choices in the game don't seem to matter all to the storyline. If they do then it only becomes apparent closer to the end of the game. More than 50 hours in and I haven't seen it impact much besides small differences in quest outcomes.
- Following the plot of the game is a challenge because its not clear who is on whose side. 
- There are so many tedious side quests.
- So ... many ... cutscenes.
- The "skills" feel too bloated. It didn't need skills that give percentage increases. Once you go down that path it just adds to the bloat.
- The music is so repetitive. The same song gets played over, and over, and over.

Verdict:

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II - A Departure from Its Roots
This isn’t Kingdom Come: Deliverance II; it feels like Embracer Group-funded fanfiction that betrays the spirit of the original. At most 6/10.
What Went Wrong?

Historical Accuracy? Vanished.
Gameplay Improvements? Barely noticeable.
Story? A disjointed mess.
RPG Elements? Reduced to a cinematic adventure game.

Gameplay: Stagnation with a Side of Simplification
The gameplay is a near-carbon copy of KCD1, but dumbed down for broader appeal. Combat feels marginally smoother, with ranged mechanics seeing slight tweaks, but it’s nowhere near a leap forward. It’s safe, uninspired, and lacks the depth to elevate the experience.

Story & RPG: A Narrative Trainwreck
The story unravels like a feverish nightmare, devoid of coherence or purpose. You begin with a simple task (deliver a letter and negotiate), but the game railroads you into a relentless series of disasters. Your choices, the heart of any RPG, are meaningless. Obvious pitfalls loom, yet Henry stumbles into them like a hapless fool, stripped of agency.
The narrative subjects Henry to a grueling 100-hour humiliation ritual: beaten, imprisoned, degraded, and lectured by caricatures. The capable agent of KCD1 is reduced to a bumbling observer, disconnected from the world and his own story. The plot feels like a betrayal when played after the first game, with events that clash jarringly and fail to build on established lore. By the end, Henry’s quest for revenge fizzles out for the most contrived reasons, leaving him aimless, hollow, and devoid of growth. He’s a shell of a protagonist with no desires beyond shallow “romance” options, no arc, and no future.

History: Sacrificed for Modern Sensibilities
The soul of Kingdom Come, its commitment to historical immersion, has been gutted. Real events are warped with fictional liberties, anachronistic elements like a synagogue appearing centuries early, and modern buzzwords that shatter the setting’s authenticity. Historical figures are misrepresented, and the game leans into heavy-handed, unquestionable narratives that feel like propaganda. Henry, and by extension the player, is forced to nod along, unable to challenge or engage with these jarring inclusions.

Final Verdict
Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a disappointment, trading the gritty, grounded charm of its predecessor for modern slop. It’s a game that forgets its roots, alienates its fans, and leaves Henry—and the player—lost in a hollow, directionless experience. But just as the bible tells us: to a starving man every bitter thing is sweet; Gamers are starving.

Very mixed feelings.  This is an extremely well done game in everything that it sets out to accomplish, from my 40 hours playing through Act 1.  However, I do not like it, and I should have done more research before buying.

If you like games like the Witcher 3, and you're interested in a semi-realistic medieval theme, then this game is likely right up your alley.  If RDR2 was tolerable but edging close to the line of too much story, then this game is probably not for you.

This is an RPG on rails where you play a pre-defined character with specific motivations.  You do get to level up various skills and can focus your character's talents to your liking, but at the end of the day you play as Henry.  Henry can either be nice or a jerk, and as expected the game changes a bit depending on how nice or mean you are.  There is one way to progress through the story, with flexibility on character advancements between the story beats.  There is some variation on how you approach missions that aren't heavily scripted, as you can be stealthy, talky, or a murderer, but it's all pretty standard fare.

The story sequences are extremely long.  I think I clocked in like 3+ hours before I was finally done with the introduction and finally had some agency to play the game freely.  I then spent around 37 hours having a reasonably good time, until I hit the next story beat.  Thankfully the game warns you that you are entering a scripted section, but looking online it seems like the next scripted section might last up to 6 hours?  No thank you; I'm officially calling it quits.

The dialog and character animations are top notch.  The quests are fairly standard but not overly fedex; some are quite fun.  I actually have a fondness for the characters and the environment, but not enough to make me spend hours on cutscenes and scripted missions.  I prefer a game in which I have considerably more agency throughout the length of the game. 

I do see how people who are into games like this absolutely love it, and defend it.  This is a very high quality game.  However, I would not recommend it to anyone who is not into this particular flavor of RPG, and those people probably already own it.

There is only one reason why I cannot recommend this game...at least for now.

And that's because of the ridiculous amount of buggy stuff going on in this game. The story is amazing, and the side quests are great, but all too often I find myself with a broken immersion when:

- I cannot really hunt well because animals move randomly af, and I mean backwards, sideways and sometimes they even fly off.

- I can't really commit crimes because NPCs are omniscient and will always blame you even if no one saw you, and if you try to stop them by killing all witnesses, they will still find out, and while chasing them they can literally teleport and go trough walls and fences.

- Mounted combat is completely broken and definitely not recommended. Despite having some perks available on the perk tree, the only viable way of fighting on a horse is from a distance and running away pretty much all the time because NPCs can run extremely fast without getting tired, even in full armor, all too often they might be even faster than your horse and then teleport to you, hit the horse and then dismount you, and charging them basically doesn't work at all.

- The DLC of the simthy is great, but every weapon that you forge literally looks the exact same. You only get to craft 3 types of things: short sword, long sword and an axe, and they all look the exact same. Even the axis that you're supposed to craft in the story quest is literally a short sword. They didn't even bother making a different mesh, not even for the main DLC quest, which feels incredibly bad, to be honest.

- And the most annoying bug of them all, happening all too often (I've already counted it 32 times in my playthrough, and that's when I started counting), is when suddenly my inventory gets bugged and I find myself in the middle of a fight, unable to change my weapon or drink any potions, even though I have them already equipped. The only way to fix this is to exit the game and re-launch it, because reloading a saved game will not fix the issue, and that means that all too often you will probably lose all your progress because of this random bug, and be unable to fight at all.

- Another mention I'd like to add is that melee combat happens on rails. You can only dodge attacks if the green shield pops up, and for some reason many times this will not happen, and enemies will hit you as if their weapons were heat seeking missiles, even if you're well outside of their range (they will literally teleport to you), which is incredibly annoying, and makes the dodging gameplay extremely unrewarding and overall, really buggy. In fact, many times you'll find yourself in a fight where you cannot win with skill, because the only way to block your enemy's attacks is by having invested enough money on your skill tree abilities with that weapon, or by training until you get a high enough level. You cannot win otherwise because your enemies will have essentially infinite stamina, strength and their attacks go towards you on rails. In the end, the best choice is a bow with poisonous arrows, which by the way is incredibly broken as well. You can down an entire army with just that.


So yeah, many people will think I'm being unfair because the game has a genuinely good story, but the game is so heavily scripted that it comes with a lot of stuff that will break the immersion, and that also makes the gameplay incredibly restrictive and linear. I'm not saying that the game is bad, all I'm saying is that it still needs a lot of work in order to feel like a polished, properly finished game, that's all.

And by the way, I'd gladly pay extra as long as this work gets properly done, after all, I've bought almost all the DLCs with the intention of supporting the developers, and trying the new content because I love the KCD series. But I really can't properly recommend this game until it's polished and released in a much better state.

I previously gave the game a thumbs up and noted that despite it's flaws, it was a good game. However, I've now lost interest in the desire to continue to play it. 

The first 50ish or so hours in the first region was pretty fun. It's challenging, the story is decent, and the game play feels fresh and different. However, upon entering the 2nd region, I've grown very tired of the repetitive time-wasting "quests" , overly drawn-out cut scenes, and the main character, Henry, gets so insanely overpowered, there's not a single fight that is fun. 

All quests are fetch, find, and talk-to quests. Quite literally. Wow, so much fun. Worse of all, every NPC encountered in the quest just drag on and on in their dialogue, it becomes mouth-droolingly boring. You can tell they attempted to design each quest as if each have their own backstory and conclusion, but you have to listen to an NPC spend 5 minutes telling you the backstory about his brother you're trying to find, only to be told you now need to go talk to other NPC's across the map to find out more. 

Once you experience this 3 or 4 times, you start to see the pattern and I started to not look forward to any of the main quest of side quests, as they're all the same. There is never anything exciting or fun in them. And worse of all, there is ABSOLUTELY NOTHING satisfying in the conclusion of the quest. EVER. You might get a few hundred coins or a cheap piece of gear. That's all you're going to get for your 1-2 hours of listening to long and drawn out NPCs yap away about characters you're not invested in. 

I think the huge main city duels is a PERFECT example and representation of how lackluster every quest is in this game. In the largest city in the game in the 2nd region, there's these -- what's supposed to be massive spectacles of dueling tournaments where the entire city comes together and watches knights duel each other in various tournaments. When I found out I could join, it was the first thing I was looking forward to do in the game so I joined it. 

The day of the tournament came and they even have a graphical cutscene as if you're about to watch a massive gladiatorial spectacle. And then the game starts and a whopping 10 or so NPCs are standing around "cheering" - which is just depicted by 3 or so voice actors randomly whistling and cheering on either you or your opponent. The duel starts and....I beat the opponent in 2 or 3 hits in the 1st round of 3 in less than 10 seconds. I did the same thing in the 2nd and final round, eventually winning the tournament. 

That was it. It was over. This entire tournament the devs attempted to conjure as a massive spectacle was nothing more than a tiny little street fight that lasted all but 3 minutes and the game pretends you just won like Spartacus in gladiator arena. THIS is a PERFECT representation of every single quest in this game. This is how it ALL feels. 

Just to make my point, in one other example - the devs defend their "Savior Schnapps" save potion saying "We once saw a suggestion from a player that it would be really cool if taverns are save points. Where you go to the tavern to hang out and drink a beer and that's how you save the game". 

Cool! Except that's not even CLOSE to what taverns are like in this game. The biggest tavern in this game never has more than 2 or 3 people actually in the tavern. You can't visually drink (you can only drink from your inventory), the audio cues for taverns make them literally dead places (with 1 or 2 people talking quietly in the background), there's no music, no band playing, no drinking parties, no yelling or bar fights, etc. Compare this to something like Skyrim or RDR2's bars. They were LIVE and fun to visit. Taverns in this game is like nearly abandoned buildings. There's nothing in them, no people in them, no action or life in them. They're boring dead places that you will never look forward to visiting. 

Everything about this game is like it was written down and sounded good on paper, but the execution was a complete failure. 

I really wish they fleshed out their ideas better as the ideas are great. But when you actually play it, you start to realize what their intention was and realize what your actual experience is an they are very far apart.

There are other ridiculous parts like being forced to help a foreign hostile religious group at the expense of your own people. Anyway, its a shame the developers of the original game were compromised.

While KCD 2 has blacksmithing and better alchemy, KCD 1 had much better world building and a far more immersive world. This game should have been a 10/10 for me as someone who bought KCD 1 Royal Edition TWICE, but I've been holding back my review because of many questionable decisions by the devs. Then I realized the fact that I have to hesitate giving an instant positive review when I am already viewing the game in rose-tinted glasses by the fact that I loved the first game so much means I have to give this game a negative review so they do not do it again.

My List among many others:
- Kuttenberg is fake big and anyone who tried to level up thievery in Kuttenberg would immediately realize that like 90% of the doors can't actually be interacted with. This makes Kuttenberg very confusing and very difficult to get immersed in. In comparison, the first map was well done. Maybe they should have just done one map if they are going to mess up the biggest city in the game. Why would you do that to Kuttenberg knowing most of the players at end game would chill in Kuttenberg?

- For a developer praised for having historically accurate buildings in KCD 1 resulting in many KCD 1 vs real life videos, not including the inside of churches in the game is a very unusual and terrible decision. Meanwhile you have Assassin's Creed Unity being praised for having a highly accurate Notre Dame.

- Badly written modern politics characters and storylines in a historically based game. Key here is badly written. I don't care what you do because I'm not interested in politics as long as it doesn't affect the immersion of the world, but you can't tell me, for example, that Musa was added properly and in good faith. Completely different religion, have to cross the Sahara Desert (the LARGEST hot desert in the world), cross the Mediterranean, then end up, not in Italy or Spain with coasts, but go all the way to a landlocked central European country. If you wanted to have a similar character, countries like Morocco, Tunis, Turkey, or Egypt wouldn't have raised any or as much eyebrows. Especially considering Morocco has the oldest university in the world. It would have been much better writing to have an educated diverse character coming directly from there for example. In addition, the North African region shares a long history with Europe such as the history between Rome and Carthage. You even have Morocco trying to join the European Communities in 1987 which shows that it considers the idea of being part of Europe. On the other hand, in games like Europa Universalis IV, you can't even really interact with Mali without getting colonizing technology as a European country or get to late game and that happens WAYYY AFTER the events of this game. Maybe it has something to do with the LARGEST HOT DESERT in the world being in the way... just a guess. I'm not claiming to be some history expert and I'm not sure I got everything 100% correct but these are just basic perfectly reasonable things and trying to give a reasonable solution is always better than just complaining. Anyone saying it is not just at the very least even a little unimmersive is just blatantly lying. Let's not pretend there aren't a billion other options for something similar and far more historically immersive before getting to Musa. And this is just one example of badly written modern politics instances.

- Something about the way the game is written and how the world was made have currently made me not have more than one playthrough. At this point, I still only have one save file. Meanwhile, in KCD 1, I have multiple save files of both hardcore and normal to the point where I have many routes to towns memorized from playing with hardcore mode such as Rattay to Talmberg, Talmberg to Pribyslavitz, Rattay to Sasau just all chilling in my head without the use of the map. I cannot say the same thing about this game.

In conclusion, I would rather have the world and storyline of the first game and just add the blacksmithing, better alchemy, and new crafting items and options such as having your own forge than the world of the second game with its terrible, unimmersive world. There are no similar games in the market so they are allowed to just mess up. Very few "immesive RPG" games even have a functionally immersive sleep mechanic much less all the other things. This game is like a room full of mirrors - there isn't any real depth, just reflections to make it seem bigger and grander than it actually is. The graphics is beautiful, the main quest line is interesting - but that's about it. 

The game is over-bloated with the most sacrificial, shallow and bland secondary quests I've seen in a long time. From the first hour of playing right till the very end, you see the same pattern: 

1. Bring something to someone. 
2. Travel across the map to fetch it. 
3. Turns out the person doesn't have it/lost it/it was stolen. 
4. Travel across the map in the other direction to retrieve it. 
5. Boring fight/search sequence. 
6. Bring it back.

It's just so repetitive, so mundane. Other key points about this game: 

- Voice acting is terrible (apart from a few exceptions, such as Capon). 
- The equipment you can get is pretty much the same as in the first game - variety is so poor! - Random forest-roaming bandits wearing some of the most expensive pieces of armour.
- Invisible walls.
- Weird narrative choices and not-so-subtle enforcement of modern political views.
- Hunting doesn't really serve a purpose.
- The world is huge but empty - those places that are more lively (like settlements) are very static, there's nothing really going on. 
- Choices have no real impact on anyone but the main protagonist.

There's an annoying lack of consistency with historical accuracy - some elements are hyper-accurate (equipment, locations, the general setting etc), and others are fitting the time/place premise very loosely (such as the whole thing with Capon getting imprisoned - it's just ridiculous).

In the end, this game isn't hugely improved from KCD 1. It looks and runs better - but it also repeats a lot of the predecessor's mistakes and misses out on easy wins and improvements. It's fun to play at times - but other times, it's anything but fun. Can't recommend.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is the ultimate Jekyll and Hyde experience. It delivers some of the best RPG content I've played in years, only to follow it up with an almost unrecognizable, massive quality drop.
Let’s be clear: the first region of KCD II is absolutely fantastic. I could easily give this section of the game a 9/10. It captures that gritty, lived-in historical atmosphere perfectly.
​The true star here isn't the main plot—it’s the people. The side quests and NPCs are genuinely rich, well-written, and often hilarious. Everything feels organic; every little interaction builds the world. I happily lost over 40 hours just messing around, learning trades, and solving local disputes, feeling like I was truly part of 15th-century Bohemia.
​The one persistent thorn is, predictably, the combat. It's still clunky, unforgiving, and often feels like fighting the controls more than the bandits. But honestly, in the first region, the strength of the world is so high that you forgive it. It’s a tolerable flaw in an otherwise stellar opening act.

And then you move to the second region. What happened?
The quality drop is massive and immediate. It’s like the development team that wrote the first part was replaced by a different studio overnight. The writing suddenly becomes sloppy and uninspired. Quests that were formerly engaging, character-driven narratives turn into boring fetch quests.
The biggest disappointment is the main city. It’s huge, but it's strangely sterile and lacks the bustling, lived-in detail that made the smaller hamlets so great. The sheer lack of compelling content makes it feel hollow.
After spending so much time invested in Henry and the incredible world of the first region, hitting this narrative wall is exhausting. The game goes from being an obsessive, can’t-put-it-down experience to a chore. I tried to force myself through, but I just couldn't. I ended up putting it down after barely scratching the surface of the second half.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II – A Suffocating Exercise in Designer Worship (2/10)

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is one of the most aggressively **railroaded** RPGs I’ve played in years. Despite marketing itself as an open-world role-playing experience, it offers almost no meaningful freedom in how you approach problems. At best, a quest allows one method of completion — if you’re lucky, two. Deviating from the designer’s narrow intent is punished, not rewarded.

This is not a game that trusts the player. It cages you.

### Illusion of Choice, Reality of Constraint

You are not encouraged to think creatively. You are not rewarded for clever approaches. You are funneled into long, rigid quest chains that feel more like chores than adventures. The game constantly forces you through tedious sequences that could and *should* be optional or skippable.

A huge portion of quests revolve around utterly joyless tasks:

* Carry this heavy bag of rice across the map.
* Deliver charcoal while moving at a crippled pace.
* Perform menial errands designed purely to consume time.

It feels less like gameplay and more like someone deliberately testing how much boredom you’ll tolerate.

### Time-Wasting as a Core Design Philosophy

Crafting is a prime example of misplaced realism:

* Sharpening a blade? 5–10 minutes.
* Brewing a potion? 5–10 minutes.
* Crafting equipment? Again, several minutes.

Every single time.

Not optional. Not accelerated. Just repetitive tedium disguised as “immersion.”

Herbalism is equally maddening. Every plant pickup triggers a small animation. One second sounds trivial, until you’re harvesting 30 plants and forced to watch the same crouch animation dozens of times in a row. In any modern RPG, this would be streamlined. Here, it's treated as sacred ritual you must endure.

### Roleplaying? Only If You Play Nice

Play as a criminal? Forget it. The game punishes this path so disproportionately that it borders on unusable. NPCs magically identify you as the culprit, guards swarm relentlessly, and social systems close off. The message is clear: behave like the moral hero or suffer mechanically.

Dialogue choices exist, but deviating from the expected personality costs you heavily. You’re not shaping a character; you’re selecting from pre-approved archetypes.

### Combat Realism That Becomes Anti-Fun

While grounded combat can be appreciated, here it becomes another tool of frustration. Fighting more than one enemy is almost always a losing proposition. Realistic? Sure. Enjoyable? Rarely. Empowering? Never.

Couple that with repeated early-game scenarios where your character loses everything and is constantly beaten down, and it borders on masochism.

### Invisible Walls and False Open Worlds

For a game claiming open-world status, the invisible walls are embarrassing. Entire areas are blocked in ways that shatter immersion and prevent exploration or creative problem-solving. Even later in the game, these barriers persist, undermining any illusion of freedom.

### Cheats as a Red Flag

There’s a saying: the more cheats a modern game needs, the more broken its core design is. Whether you agree or not, the fact remains — a significant portion of this game's community relies on cheats to bypass its frustrations, not enhance fun. That alone speaks volumes.

### The Verdict

Yes, the writing is fine. The combat is serviceable.

But the fundamental design philosophy is hostile to the player.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is slow, rigid, unforgiving, and obsessively committed to wasting your time in the name of faux realism. It does not respect player autonomy, creativity, or time investment.

If you want:

* Freedom in quest-solving
* Meaningful choice
* A modern RPG experience
* Efficient gameplay
* Respect for your time

Avoid this game.

**Final score: 2/10**

I want to preface my review by saying that overall I think it is a fine game, BUT this game is massively flawed and I feel a lot of the reviews are being dishonest about how glaring those flaws are when they call it a 9 or 10/10. 

Firstly, all of the things about the graphics, combat, and exploration you have heard are correct. This is a beautifully crafted world that is a joy to explore and get lost in. which is why it is so unfortunate the game rips you out of that and forces you to experience the worst chain of quests that I have ever experienced in a video game. I wish that were me being hyperbolic, but it is not. Minor spoiler, but there is a chain of three quests that are unskippable and cannot be interrupted with exploration or any manner of other distraction. These are main story quests that you must complete before you get back to what this game truly excels at. The developers got high one day and decided that the monastery quest from the first game needed a even grander more annoying sequel, and put two nearly back to back forced stealth sections, and follow it up with a quest that rips all choice away from you to complete it without feeling the need to throw your PC through the wall, or ripping your own hair out. My recommendation is to keep a guide open through this to shorten the amount of time you waste. I have genuinely no idea how any of the reviews I watched or read failed to mention the six hour unskippable hell this game puts you through to continue with the rest of the game. I will say that this is clearly all my own opinion, but this game has slowly killed any desire to replay it, as I will not subject myself to this torture for a second time.

Also, another thing that really bothers me in this game, is you are basically required to use the thievery skill, as most of the side quests in the game require some form of lock picking or pick pocketing to complete, including the brushes with death dlc. The quest design in this game forces you to play a certain way if you want to even remotely interact with like 60% of what it has to offer. The last thing I wanted to be doing was be forced to play a thief in a game about medieval knights. If I wanted to play a thief, I'd play Thief. 

in conclusion, I would rate this game a solid 6/10, but falls very short of the hype that surrounds this game, and leaves me deeply disappointed in the reviewers who so clearly ignored the glaring flaws in what could only be called a decent game

I have finished the game now, so here are my complete thoughts on it:
I really want to like this game, but there were a lot of things that put me off of it.

Quality of life is worse than KCD1. They added more systems to take away from player time, resources, and fun. For example, herbs can now expire like food.

Combat is worse than KCD1 IMO. Early level combat feels impossible, more impossible than any low level combat that I encountered in KCD1. Even at level 14 with master strike and training, it's nigh impossible to take on two armored bandits with my dog. Having now completed the game, it feels like the game is centered around late-game combat even though it only takes up a small portion of the game.

'For Whom the Bells Toll' is the single-worst quest design that I've ever encountered. I hated that quest and I hated monastery in KCD1. Stealth from one end of this place to the other, oh I need this thing that's back from where you started, go all the way back then come all the way back to me. 

There are a lot of bugs and crashing for me personally. One of the worst bugs is that I'm getting trespassed in rooms that I already paid for, effectively taking my money and rescinding on the paid service. In the second region, I've crashed half a dozen times. Throughout the game I also encountered floating NPCs, combat camera getting stuck looking anywhere except the enemy, locking onto enemies not working properly, and one specific guard on a mission spotting me from behind a wall, 40ft away, behind him, when you proc him with proximity to move for a certain quest.

It feels impossible for me to know what level I should be or what level of equipment I should have before I invest way too much of my time in a quest that I'll just have to reload 10 saves before to finish later (INHALE) because my stats/equipment aren't up to par. Ultimately I think this comes down to the game focusing too much on end-game play and not enough on early-level fun. 

I will say that the game was much more fun late-game for the reasons I mentioned before about it feeling focused around that. The story got much better towards the end. I felt invested in my companions and allies towards the end of the game, and their personalities each shown through. I had a lot more fun with the combat and skills late-game.

*Spoiler ahead*:

After 190 hours in the game, I have to say I’m very disappointed. To be fair to Warhorse, the Trosky part is a solid 10/10. Kuttenberg up to the Italian heist and Suchdol remains consistent and emotionally gripping.

But after the Maleshov battle, the quality drops hard. The tone turns soft, with the casualties of multiple life and death battles reduced to only one cutthroat, Adder, dying in a sentimental cutscene. It feels exactly like a Disney or Marvel movie, and a bad one at that.

In a war story, that’s laughable. Where’s the sacrifice? Where’s the brutality? This is supposed to be Bohemia in 1403, not a safe fairytale. I see no problem with killing more fictional characters like Kubyenka, Katherine, Godwin or even Capon anyone except Žižka who is a historical figure. In fact, it could have made for a far heavier and more compelling final arc for Henry, with him seeking revenge, if Brabant’s betrayal had happened during the Maleshov battle instead of afterward. It also would have been more logical with Brabant acting as a spy, deliberately sabotaging the cannon operation, and surrounding the crew with unreliable mercenaries.

It would have ended much better with brutal casualties at Maleshov, rather than dragging on into the unrealistic and unhistorical gta 5 style Italian Court heist and Suchdol siege, both entirely wrong historically and seemingly added just for the sake of gameplay.

Warhorse had a chance to make us feel the cost and risk of war, to let death weigh heavy, to show us rage, loss, and blood. Instead, they dulled the blade, and what could have been a lasting, gut punch finale turned into something shallow and weightless like a Hollywood movie.

P.S. Most romances in KCD2 feel like glorified one night stands, with Rosa and other options resulting in a single scene and barely registering afterward. Katherine is sometimes cited as an exception, but even she only gets a single notable moment. In KCD1, Theresa’s romance felt more developed and personal, with dialogue and actions that built a sense of history and mutual care. In KCD2, we lack that depth entirely, and worse, we are never given the choice to reject advances beforehand. Rosa is the prime example: she behaves with incredible arrogance despite her supposed “help” during the tunneling sequence : "help" which we could have completely managed ourselves. In KCD1, Henry was capable of finding and navigating far more difficult and elusive locations without hand-holding, so her involvement feels unnecessary and forced. Many characters lack depth, defaulting to endless chatter without revealing anything worth caring about. This is compounded by quest design that constantly casts Henry as a glorified errand boy, because apparently no one in Bohemia can solve a problem without him. It is also entirely possible to complete the main story while skipping large swaths of optional interactions, which leaves most of the cast feeling forgettable and underdeveloped by the time the credits roll
